tagline.text: The Philippines' first Ramsar wetland, where migratory birds rest across from Mactan

children.text: A 20-minute boat ride from Mactan Island, this quiet coral island is where migratory birds from Siberia and northern China spend the winter. Designated the Philippines' first Ramsar wetland in 1994, its wildlife sanctuary, mangroves, and crystal-clear seagrass flats offer a refreshing half-day break from a resort itinerary.
Olango Island is a low, flat coral island about
5km

east of Mactan Island. The main island of Olango, together with smaller islands including Hilutungan, Nalusuan, Caohagan, and Sulpa, forms the Olango Island Group, most of which falls under Lapu-Lapu City, with part in Cordova. Though always visible across the water from Mactan's large resort strip, tourism development here has been minimal, leaving intact the simple scenery of fishing villages, seaweed farms, and narrow country lanes.

What makes Olango special is its birds. The wide mudflats, seagrass flats, and mangrove forests along the island's south coast form an important stopover on the East Asian–Australasian Flyway, where flocks of sandpipers, plovers, and egrets from Siberia, northern China, and Japan stop to feed while escaping winter. In
, about 920 hectares of mudflats were designated the Olango Island Wildlife Sanctuary, and in

it became the Philippines' first Ramsar wetland. About 97 bird species have been recorded here to date, roughly half of them migratory, including endangered species such as the Chinese egret, great knot, and Far Eastern curlew.
The island is so low it doesn't rise more than

above sea level, and it is ringed by wide coral reefs and seagrass beds. At high tide, clear seawater rises to the end of the sanctuary's walkway and mirrors the sky, while at low tide endless tidal flats are exposed and birds scatter to feed. On the east shore, bamboo floating restaurants sit on the water, and it's fun to go out by boat and eat seafood there.

For birdwatchers and nature photographers, it's the closest migratory bird site to Cebu; for general travelers, it's a half-day escape not far from the Mactan resorts, offering a taste of everyday Filipino fishing-village life and a quiet sea. Rather than expecting a glamorous beach or amenities, think of it as a place to slow down, circling the island by bicycle or tricycle.

After entering through the sanctuary office in Barangay San Vicente on the island's south side, you can watch flocks of migratory birds from the boardwalk stretching over the mudflats and from observation decks. Bring binoculars to see the sandpipers' bill shapes and the egrets' feathers up close.

The boardwalk winding through the mangrove forest out toward the sea feels as though it's on the verge of being submerged at high tide, giving the sensation of walking on water. On calm days, the sky and clouds reflect on the surface for beautiful photos.

The water in front of the sanctuary is shallow and clear enough to see the seagrass swaying on the bottom. Watching small fish, crabs, and starfish while wading through the shallows is a distinctive experience.
One of Cebu Province's largest mangrove forests lines the island's south coast. Crabs and mudskippers move among the exposed roots, and the dense shade makes it a good place to rest even at midday.

Off the coast of Caw-oy village on the island's east side are floating restaurants, bamboo huts set afloat on the sea. Taking a small boat out to a hut, ordering shrimp, crab, clams, and grilled fish, and eating in the middle of the sea is a highlight of an Olango trip.

blocks.title: Circling the Island by Bicycle or Tricycle

children.text: The whole island is flat, making it easy to explore by bicycle. Riding past fishing villages, seaweed drying in the sun, small chapels, and schools offers a close-up view of island life entirely different from the city.

Coral reef walls line the island's west and north coasts, offering several dive sites, and the Hilutungan and Nalusuan marine sanctuaries — popular stops on Mactan hopping tours — also belong to the Olango Island Group.

For birdwatching,
September–April
is best. Early arrivals begin showing up from
August
, with numbers said to peak during
October–November
, as birds move south, and again in
February–March
, as they gather before heading back north. From
May to July

, most migratory birds have left for their breeding grounds, leaving mainly resident species. Migration timing shifts somewhat from year to year, so check recent sighting reports from the sanctuary office or a local birdwatching group.
For weather,
January–May
brings the least rain and calmest seas. Lying between Mactan and Bohol, Olango is relatively sheltered from typhoons, but during the
June–November
rainy season, showers are frequent, and strong winds can halt the ferry. Midday temperatures generally run around
, feeling even hotter on the shade-poor mudflats, so birdwatching is best done early in the morning or late afternoon.

Most travelers stay at a Mactan resort or in Cebu City and visit Olango for half a day. To spend a night and try dawn birdwatching, small dive resorts or guesthouses on the island's coast (about

a night) are an option. Convenience stores and restaurants are scarce, and the whole island, being a coral island, has limited fresh water, so facilities are basic — but you'll get a quiet night away from Mactan's noise.

Olango's signature food is seafood straight from the sea. At the Caw-oy floating restaurants, you choose shrimp, crab, shellfish, or fish from tanks or baskets, pay by weight, and have it grilled, steamed, or made into soup. Also try kinilaw (fish cured in vinegar) and coconut-milk seafood stews. Small eateries and sari-sari stores on the island serve cheap carinderia-style meals of rice and side dishes, and back on Mactan, resorts and sutukil restaurants offer dinner options.
Be sure to check the tide table. Birds gather near the observation decks around high tide and scatter too far away to see clearly with the naked eye at low tide.
Binoculars and a telephoto lens multiply the enjoyment of birdwatching. A wide-brimmed hat and sunscreen are also essential.
Inside the sanctuary, don't approach the birds closely or make noise, and don't fly a drone — a startled flock can take off all at once.
There are almost no ATMs on the island. Bring enough cash for the ferry, entrance fee, tricycle, and meals.
Before ordering at a floating restaurant, confirm the seafood's price per kilogram and any separate cooking fee.
When walking the seagrass flats, wear aqua shoes, as sea urchins and sharp coral fragments may be present.
Confirm the last return boat time as soon as you arrive, and be back at the pier at least
1 hour
before sunset.
The Caw-oy floating restaurants were all destroyed or washed away during Typhoon Odette in
December 2021
, and only some owners have rebuilt since. Before you go, ask your tricycle driver or accommodation which ones are open now, and if they're closed, eat at the carinderias around Santa Rosa pier.
Boats back to Mactan stop around sunset, and service is suspended if winds are strong. Check the last boat time and weather in advance so you're not stranded on the island.
Collecting or disturbing birds, nests, shellfish, and seagrass is prohibited in the sanctuary. Take all your trash with you.
If you walk far out onto the mudflats at low tide, the incoming tide can rise quickly and make it hard to get back. Don't stray far from the designated boardwalk.
Shade and stalls are scarce on the island, creating a heatstroke risk at midday. Bring plenty of water.
Fix tricycle and outrigger-boat fares before boarding, and compare prices if a tout offers an expensive private tour.
Tap water on the island may not be suitable for drinking. Drink bottled water instead.
